items.answer: Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.

Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

A virtual reality system is a system that presents a computer-generated artificial environment, provides computer-generated sensory stimuli for an immersive experience, and lets the user's actions partially determine what happens in it.

A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

questions.question: Which three components make up the complete view of a virtual reality system?
options: the organism, the virtual environment, and the surrounding physical world
the organism, the VR software, and the surrounding physical world
the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world
the VR hardware, the virtual environment, and the surrounding physical world
questions.explanation: The complete view of a VR system includes the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world. The virtual environment and software are not the three system components in that view.

questions.question: In the complete view of a virtual reality system, what is the flow of data from the VR hardware to the organism called?
options: rendering
feedback
tracking
stimulation
questions.explanation: Stimulation is the hardware-to-organism data flow. Tracking is the opposite direction, from the organism to the VR hardware.

questions.question: What makes the organism component unavoidable in the complete view of a virtual reality system?
options: a surrounding physical world that is always present
a virtual environment that is always present
a VR hardware set that is always present
a human user who is always present
questions.explanation: The organism cannot be omitted because the human user is always present and is as important to account for as the VR hardware. The other components are not the organism itself.

data.text: A complete VR system includes the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world, not hardware alone. These parts are linked by data flows: tracking from the organism to VR hardware, stimulation from VR hardware to the organism, and bidirectional flows between the physical world and both the VR hardware and the organism. The organism is therefore an essential component to account for alongside the VR hardware.
points: A complete view of a VR system includes the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world.
Tracking flows organism to VR hardware; stimulation flows VR hardware to organism; the physical world has bidirectional flows with both.
The organism, usually the human user, is as important as VR hardware and cannot be omitted; it is always present.

questions.question: In a VR system, what does the data flow from the VR equipment to the user carry?
options: real-world ambient sounds
tracked presses of buttons
sensed motions of the user
hardware-generated sensory inputs
questions.explanation: The hardware-to-user flow carries hardware-generated stimuli for the user's senses. The other options describe tracked user actions or sounds from the physical world, not hardware-generated stimulation.

questions.question: Which tracking is the most important thing to track in a VR system?
options: eye movement tracking
controller movement tracking
head tracking
body-part movement tracking
questions.explanation: Head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track in VR. Eye movements, controller movements, and other body-part movements may also be tracked, but they are not the most important tracking.

data.text: A VR system is described at the systems level by the way hardware and user are connected through data flows. One flow carries stimulation data that overrides the senses, while the other carries tracking data that lets the hardware adjust the stimuli. Tracking is commonly centered on the head, but it can also include button presses, controller movements, eye movements, and other body movements.
points: VR hardware and user exchange a stimulation data flow overriding senses and a tracking data flow adjusting stimuli from motion.
VR systems commonly track head most importantly, and can track button presses, controller movements, eye movements, and body movements.

questions.question: How can the surrounding physical environment affect a user's behavior while interacting with a virtual world?
options: The user may respond to tracked user movements such as hand, head, and body motion
The user may respond to hardware output such as display images and controller vibration
The user may respond to real-world stimuli such as light, sound, and smell
The user may respond to virtual-world stimuli such as light, sound, and smell
questions.explanation: The surrounding physical environment can affect the user because the user may still respond to real-world stimuli and may not be fully detached from the real world. Virtual-world stimuli and hardware output are part of the intended VR experience rather than the real-world environment.

questions.question: Why might VR hardware track objects in the surrounding physical environment rather than the user directly?
options: When interaction with those objects is part of the experience
When the surrounding physical environment contains real-world landmarks
When the virtual scene needs a larger field of view than the display provides
When the user's head movements are too fast for the sensors
questions.explanation: VR hardware may track physical objects directly when the experience requires interaction with those objects. Tracking is not primarily a workaround for slow sensors, display limits, or landmarks.

questions.question: How can VR hardware that includes a robotic arm affect the surrounding physical environment?
options: By displaying virtual images on surfaces in that environment
By recording the movement of objects in that environment
By sending recorded sound to the user's headphones
By changing the position of objects in that environment
questions.explanation: A robotic arm is an example of VR hardware that can change the physical environment, such as by moving objects, and that change may affect the user. Displaying images, recording motion, or sending sound does not describe this environmental change.

questions.question: What may VR hardware include beyond the computer, head-mounted display, and controller used by the user?
options: The user's tracked hand movements
The surrounding physical environment itself
Objects in the surrounding physical environment
The virtual room rendered on the display
questions.explanation: VR hardware is not limited to the computer, HMD, or controller; it may deal with objects in the surrounding physical environment. The environment itself is a separate system component, and rendered virtual content or user movements are not hardware objects.

data.text: A VR system is not just the user and the display or controllers; it also includes the surrounding physical environment. Real-world stimuli can affect the user, and the user's physical movement can change that environment. VR hardware can therefore act beyond the user's own body and devices by tracking or changing objects in the physical environment, which can in turn influence user behavior.
points: A virtual reality system includes the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment.
The surrounding physical environment is part of the VR system because real-world stimuli may affect the user's behavior.
A user's physical movement while interacting with the virtual world may change the surrounding physical environment.
VR hardware may track surrounding objects rather than the user, especially when interacting with them is part of the experience.
VR hardware may change the surrounding physical environment, affecting user behavior, and is not limited to the user's computer, HMD, or controller.

questions.question: A VR setup uses a hand device that makes the user's fingers feel pressure. Which hardware role does that device fill?
options: An output device
A processing device
A physical environment device
An input device
questions.explanation: VR output devices are defined broadly as devices that produce output that stimulates the user's sensory organs, so a device that makes fingers feel pressure is output hardware rather than tracking or processing hardware.

questions.question: A VR setup uses a device that follows the user's head motion. Why can that device be counted as VR input hardware?
options: It tracks the user's movements and extracts real-world information
It runs computations that make the virtual scene perceivable
It keeps the user responsive to physical surroundings
It presents virtual feedback that reaches the user's senses
questions.explanation: In VR hardware, input devices are sensors that track the user's movements and extract information from the real world. Following head motion fits that tracking role, not producing or processing sensory experience.

questions.question: Which VR hardware component is responsible for turning tracked input into perceivable virtual output?
options: The display
The physical environment
The sensor
The computer
questions.explanation: The computer is the processing device: it processes inputs and produces outputs for the user to perceive the virtual world. Displays provide sensory output, sensors track input, and the physical environment is part of the overall system rather than a processing component.

data.text: VR hardware is organized into three functional parts: displays, sensors, and computers. These terms are used broadly: a display produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs, a sensor tracks the user's movement and extracts information from the real world, and a computer processes inputs to produce outputs for the user to perceive the world. Together they describe how VR hardware produces output, captures user movement, and processes inputs for perception.
points: VR hardware has three major components: displays, sensors, and computers.
In VR hardware, a display is broadly any output device stimulating the user's sensory organs.
In VR hardware, a sensor is broadly any tracking device that tracks the user's movement and extracts real-world information.
In VR hardware, a computer is broadly any processing device that produces outputs from inputs for the user to perceive.

questions.question: Why can a non-tracked handheld controller cause a break-in presence?
options: The user's real hand movement may not produce a matching virtual hand movement
The user's real body movement may not produce a matching virtual body movement
The user's real eye movement may not produce a matching virtual gaze movement
The user's real head movement may not produce a matching virtual head movement
questions.explanation: A non-tracked handheld controller is not positioned in 3D space, so the user's actual hand motion may not be mirrored by the virtual hands. Head, eye, and body movement are different input channels and are not the stated cause of this break-in presence.

questions.question: What limitation does a tracked handheld controller have for interacting with passive virtual objects?
options: The hands are constrained to a fixed area, so direct touch is not fully possible
The hands are exposed for a long time, so direct touch is not fully possible
The hands are held in front of a sensor, so direct touch is not fully possible
The hands are occupied with the controller, so direct touch is not fully possible
questions.explanation: Tracked handheld controllers occupy the hands, so users cannot directly or fully touch passive virtual objects through tangible interaction. Long exposure, line-of-sight requirements, and gesture memorization are issues associated with other input types, not the main limitation of tracked controllers.

questions.question: What is the main sensor difference between bend-sensing data gloves and pinch gloves?
options: Bend-sensing gloves place sensors at many joints, while pinch gloves place sensors mainly at fingertips
Bend-sensing gloves place sensors mainly at fingertips, while pinch gloves place sensors at many joints
Bend-sensing gloves place sensors on the head, while pinch gloves place sensors on the hands
Bend-sensing gloves place sensors in a head-mounted display, while pinch gloves place sensors in a handheld controller
questions.explanation: Bend-sensing data gloves use sensors at many bend positions or joints, while pinch gloves place sensors at fingertip positions to detect a limited set of pinch gestures. The other options misplace the sensors or reverse the two glove types.

questions.question: How can a bare-hand input device translate a user's hand gestures into virtual commands?
options: A fixed joystick can send position data, a computer can record the data, and software can convert the data into gestures
EMG electrodes can read muscle activity, a band can send the signals, and software can convert the signals into gestures
Infrared LEDs can illuminate the hands, cameras can capture the reflected light, and software can convert the signals into gestures
Buttons can send press events, a controller can send the events, and software can convert the events into gestures
questions.explanation: A bare-hand input device can use computer vision, such as infrared LEDs and cameras, to detect hand gestures and convert them into commands. EMG bands, buttons, and joysticks are other input approaches, not the mechanism described for bare-hand tracking.

data.text: Hand-based VR input devices are organized by how much they rely on tracked hardware, worn sensors, or the user's own hands. World-grounded and handheld controllers trade mobility, tracking accuracy, or direct touch, while hand-worn devices give richer gestures but bring calibration and comfort issues. Bare-hand tracking is the most natural option, though vision-based tracking still has line-of-sight and fatigue limits.
points: VR input devices are hand or non-hand; hand input devices have five broad categories.
World-grounded VR hand input devices are fixed in the real world, limiting the user's movement area.
Non-tracked handheld controllers can break presence, while tracked handheld controllers know position but can limit direct virtual touch.
Hand-worn VR input devices offer natural, rich gestures but may need learned gestures and can cause discomfort.
Bare-hand VR input, exemplified by Leap Motion, uses computer vision but needs line of sight and can cause fatigue.

activities.title: Order the stages of infrared hand tracking in a Leap Motion device

items.title: Order the stages of infrared hand tracking in a Leap Motion device
steps: Three IR LEDs emit IR light
IR light reflects from the user's hands
Two wide-angle cameras pick up the reflected light
Software converts the camera signals into gestures

questions.question: In VR, which signal source characterizes a non-hand-based input device?
options: a handheld controller operated by the hand as input
a fixed joystick as input
a tracked trigger as input
body parts other than the hand as input
questions.explanation: A non-hand-based input device captures input from body parts other than the hand, such as the head, eyes, voice, or body. Handheld controllers, joysticks, and triggers are hand-based input sources.

questions.question: In what way can a head-mounted display also act as a head-tracking input device?
options: by detecting yaw, roll, and pitch with its sensors
by detecting hand gestures with its sensors
by detecting button and trigger presses with its sensors
by detecting controller shakes with its sensors
questions.explanation: An HMD can double as a head-tracking device when its sensors detect head motion, especially yaw, roll, and pitch, and use that motion to change the view. Button presses, hand gestures, and controller shakes are not the head-motion signal described.

questions.question: What signal does a headset-integrated sensor capture when it helps the system infer the action the user is taking?
options: the direction of the head and its movement
the direction of the eyes and their movement
the direction of the controllers and their movement
the direction of the hands and their movement
questions.explanation: Eye-tracking sensors track where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, which helps the system infer the intended action. Head, hand, and controller movement are different input signals.

questions.question: Why can an eye-tracking-only input system accidentally perform an action?
options: because a background sound can be read as an intentional selection
because a head turn can be read as an intentional selection
because a blank gaze can be read as an intentional selection
because a quick eye blink can be read as an intentional selection
questions.explanation: The Midas touch problem occurs when eye tracking cannot tell an intentional selection gaze from a habitual blank gaze, so the system may select or act without the user's intent. Blinks, head turns, and background sounds are not the described cause.

questions.question: Why is multimodal input generally preferable over relying on a single channel for selection?
options: because hand-only input can cause accidental actions
because voice-only input can cause accidental actions
because eye-only input can cause accidental actions
because head-only input can cause accidental actions
questions.explanation: Multimodal input adds other input forms to eye tracking because eye tracking alone can select objects or perform actions from unintentional gazes. Accidental actions from hand, voice, or head-only input are not the stated reason.

data.text: Non-hand-based VR input captures input from body parts other than the hand, such as head, eyes, voice, or body movement. Head tracking uses a head-mounted display's yaw, roll, and pitch sensors to change the view, while eye tracking infers actions from eye movement. Eye tracking's Midas touch problem, confusing intentional and habitual blank gaze, makes multimodal input generally preferable.
points: Non-hand-based input devices capture input from body parts other than the hand, including head, eyes, voice, or body movement.
Head-tracking input devices typically use a head-mounted display's yaw, roll, and pitch sensors to change the view from head motion.
Eye-tracking devices integrated with headsets track where and how a user's eyes move to infer an action.
The Midas touch problem is eye tracking's confusion of intentional and habitual blank gaze, making multimodal input generally preferable.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of understanding VR hardware together with the other system components?
options: Measuring the degree to which the environment surrounds the user
Distinguishing non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems
Revealing the requirements and the hardware to look for
Selecting the interaction technique that best preserves presence
questions.explanation: Considering the whole system shows how the components interact with the hardware, which reveals the requirements and the hardware to look for. Classifying immersion or measuring presence is not the purpose described.

questions.question: What are the three major hardware components of a virtual reality system?
options: Input, output, and storage
Input, output, and processor
Display, controller, and processor
Input, display, and rendering
questions.explanation: The three major hardware components are the broad parts that handle user actions, present stimuli, and process the system. Specific devices or computer parts such as storage are not the three major categories.

data.text: Virtual reality hardware is considered within the full virtual reality system, including how the system's components interact with the hardware. That whole-system view helps identify the requirements and the hardware to look for, and it frames the main hardware categories as input, output, and processor.
points: Virtual reality hardware must be understood from the whole system's viewpoint to identify requirements and the hardware to look for.
The three major hardware components of any virtual reality system are input, output, and processor.

questions.question: Why is the surrounding physical environment included in a complete view of a virtual reality system, rather than only the user and hardware?
questions.reference_answer: A complete view of a virtual reality system consists of the organism, the virtual reality hardware, and the surrounding physical environment. The surrounding physical environment is included because the user may still respond to real-world stimuli such as light, sound, and smell, so the environment can affect user behavior. The user's physical movement may change the environment, and virtual reality hardware may also change it, for example by using a robotic arm.

questions.question: Why can a tracked handheld controller help preserve presence better than a non-tracked handheld controller in a VR system?
questions.reference_answer: A non-tracked handheld controller is not tracked in three-dimensional space, so the system does not know its exact position with respect to a reference frame. Therefore, the user's untracked hand movements may not produce corresponding changes in the virtual hands, which can cause break-in presence. A tracked handheld controller has six degrees of freedom tracking, so the system can track its movements and avoid that mismatch.

questions.question: Why is multimodal input generally preferable to relying only on eye tracking for selecting objects or performing actions in a VR system?
questions.reference_answer: Eye tracking alone can cause the Midas touch problem, where the system cannot differentiate an intentional gaze meant to select an object from a habitual blank gaze. As a result, objects may be selected or actions performed even though the user did not intend to. Multimodal input is generally preferable because it uses other forms of input in addition to eye tracking, rather than relying on eye tracking alone.
